notes.meaning: Gabriel explains that he stood beside Darius the Mede in his first year to help and protect him. This continued the heavenly battle mentioned in chapter 10, showing that God sends his angels to guide earthly rulers and keep his promises to his people. God works behind the scenes of world politics to care for his church.

The heavenly messenger reveals what will happen next in world history. Three more kings would rule Persia after Cyrus, followed by a fourth king who would be far wealthier than the others. This fourth king, Xerxes, used his great riches to gather a massive army and launch an attack against Greece.

A powerful king will step onto the world stage, ruling with huge authority and conquering whatever he chooses. This describes Alexander the Great of Greece, who overthrew the Persian Empire with amazing speed. Human rulers may feel unstoppable, but God already knows their limits.

Just when this Greek ruler reached the height of his power, his empire was suddenly broken apart. Alexander died young, and his kingdom was not passed down to his children, who were soon killed. Instead, his vast realm was split in four directions among his top generals.

The ruler of the southern territory, Ptolemy in Egypt, grew very strong. However, one of Alexander's commanders, Seleucus, became even stronger and established the Syrian empire to the north. These two rival kingdoms would clash for generations, right around the Jewish homeland.

Years later, the two dynasties tried to make peace through a royal marriage. Princess Berenice came from Egypt in the south to marry Antiochus II of Syria in the north. The political deal collapsed when the king abandoned her, and Berenice, her child, and her servants were all murdered.

A relative from the murdered queen's own family rose up to take the throne in Egypt. This was her brother, Ptolemy III, who marched a large army north to avenge her death. He invaded Syria, captured their strongholds, and defeated the northern forces.

The victorious Egyptian king carried away massive amounts of loot, including thousands of metal idols and valuable gold and silver dishes. He returned to Egypt with these sacred treasures that Persia had stolen years earlier, winning great praise from his people. After this triumph, he stayed away from war with the northern king for several years.

The king of the North tried to strike back by launching an invasion of Egypt. His military campaign failed to accomplish anything lasting, and he had to retreat to his own land. Even powerful rulers cannot win victories outside of God's timing.

The sons of the northern king rallied their kingdom to seek revenge. One of them, Antiochus the Great, swept southward like an overflowing river, taking back lost cities in Syria and Palestine. He pushed his battle lines all the way to the Egyptian border fortress of Raphia.

Enraged by this sudden invasion, the king of Egypt marched out to defend his borders. Antiochus the Great had gathered a huge army, but God had determined the outcome, and the northern army was completely crushed. The Egyptian ruler won a sweeping victory at the Battle of Raphia.

After capturing the enemy army and killing tens of thousands of soldiers, the king of Egypt became full of pride. Instead of pressing his advantage to secure lasting peace, he went back to a life of luxury and laziness. Because of his foolish arrogance, his moment of triumph slipped away without strengthening his kingdom.

Years later, the king of the North returned to finish what he started. Knowing that Egypt was now weak under a young child king, Antiochus raised an army even larger than the first, equipped with massive supplies. Earthly rivalries never stay quiet for long when greedy rulers seek power.

Many groups joined forces against the young king of Egypt during this crisis, including rebels from within Egypt and foreign allies. Some violent Jewish men also revolted, thinking they were fulfilling prophecy and gaining freedom by siding with Syria. Their rebellion came to nothing, and they were defeated.

Antiochus marched south, built siege ramps against the heavily defended city of Sidon, and captured it. The Egyptian army and its finest elite soldiers could not hold their ground and were forced to surrender. Human strength and military preparation fail when God allows an empire to fall.

The northern invader took complete control of the region, doing whatever he wanted without anyone standing in his way. He took possession of the Beautiful Land, which is Israel, bringing trouble and foreign domination to God's people. Even though the king favored some Jewish leaders, his rule placed the land under foreign subjection.

Antiochus wanted to conquer all of Egypt, but he decided to use trickery instead of open war. He arranged for his daughter Cleopatra to marry the young Egyptian king, hoping she would secretly help him take over the nation. His scheme failed because his daughter remained loyal to her new husband and Egypt instead of her father.

Turning away from Egypt, Antiochus sailed a fleet toward the Mediterranean coastlands and captured many islands and cities in Greece and Asia Minor. His arrogant advance provoked Rome, and a Roman commander named Scipio defeated him soundly in battle. The shame and insult Antiochus tried to bring upon others fell right back on his own head.

Crushed by Rome and forced to pay enormous fines, Antiochus retreated back into his own fortified cities. Desperate for money to pay the Romans, he attempted to loot a pagan temple in Elymais and was killed by the angry local citizens. His grand ambitions ended in total disgrace and sudden death.

The next king to take the northern throne was Seleucus IV, who sent an official named Heliodorus to squeeze heavy taxes from his subjects and plunder the Jerusalem temple. His rule lasted only a short time, and he was quickly killed through secret poison and treason, rather than in battle. Rulers who burden the poor and dishonor God's house do not last.

In his place arose a contemptible man named Antiochus Epiphanes, who had no rightful claim to the royal crown. He did not win the kingdom through open warfare, but slipped in during a time of ease and seized the throne through flattery and deceit. This wicked ruler would become one of the fiercest oppressors the Jewish people ever faced.

Large armies that opposed Antiochus were swept away and shattered like an overwhelming flood. During this time, a prince of the covenant was also broken and removed. This was fulfilled when the godly high priest Onias III was stripped of his sacred office and later murdered through Antiochus's plots.
